In [[queueing theory]], a discipline within the mathematical [[probability theory|theory of probability]], a '''fluid limit''', '''fluid approximation''' or '''fluid analysis''' of a stochastic model is a deterministic real-valued process which approximates the evolution of a given stochastic process, usually subject to some scaling or limiting criteria.

Fluid limits were first introduced by Thomas G. Kurtz publishing a [[law of large numbers]] and [[central limit theorem]] for [[Markov chain]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Pakdaman | first1 = K. | last2 = Thieullen | first2 = M. | last3 = Wainrib | first3 = G. | doi = 10.1239/aap/1282924062 | title = Fluid limit theorems for stochastic hybrid systems with application to neuron models | journal = Advances in Applied Probability | volume = 42 | issue = 3 | pages = 761 | year = 2010 | arxiv = 1001.2474}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Kurtz | first1 = T. G. | year = 1971 | title = Limit Theorems for Sequences of Jump Markov Processes Approximating Ordinary Differential Processes | journal = Journal of Applied Probability  | volume = 8 | issue = 2 | pages = 344–356 | publisher = Applied Probability Trust | jstor = 3211904 }}</ref> It is known that a queueing network can be stable, but have an unstable fluid limit.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Bramson | first1 = M. | title = A stable queueing network with unstable fluid model | doi = 10.1214/aoap/1029962815 | journal = The Annals of Applied Probability | volume = 9 | issue = 3 | pages = 818 | year = 1999 | jstor = 2667284| doi-access = free }}</ref>
